title: The Khasa Malla Kingdom: Nepal's Forgotten Empire
meta_description: The Khasa Malla kingdom ruled western Nepal and western Tibet from Sinja near Jumla: its kings, its capital, the Dullu pillar and the birth of Nepali.
summary: From about the 12th to the 14th century, the Khasa Malla kings ruled a Himalayan state from the Sinja valley near Jumla that stretched from western Tibet to the hills of central Nepal. Their language became Nepali. Their pillars, temples and inscriptions still stand at Sinja, Dullu, Surkhet and even Lumbini.

sections.heading: An empire most visitors have never heard of
paras: Ask a visitor about Nepal's history and you will hear about the Newar kings of the Kathmandu Valley, the pagodas of Patan and Bhaktapur, and Prithvi Narayan Shah's unification in the 18th century. Very few will mention the Khasa Mallas. Yet for about two centuries the most powerful state in the central Himalaya was ruled not from Kathmandu but from a small valley in Karnali, the Sinja valley near present-day Jumla.

At its height in the 14th century, the Khasa kingdom held land from Purang and Guge in western Tibet, around the sacred mountain of Kailash, south and east across the Karnali basin to Dullu in Dailekh and as far as Kaski in the Gandaki hills. Its armies raided the Kathmandu Valley more than once. Its kings patronised Buddhist monasteries in Tibet and Hindu temples in the hills. Then, within a few generations, it broke apart into small states, and its story slipped out of the history most Nepalis learn at school.

Travelling in the far west today, you meet the Khasa world constantly without always knowing it: in the stone pillars by the roadside, the square stone shrines called dewal, the water spouts carved with inscriptions, and in the Nepali language itself.

sections.heading: Kings and dates
paras: The dynasty's history is pieced together from inscriptions, copper plates, Tibetan records and the chronicles of the Kathmandu Valley. Dates are often approximate, and historians still debate details. What follows are the rulers most often named in the sources.

sections.heading: Sinja: the capital in the hills
paras: Sinja lies along the Hima river in Jumla district, at about 2,490 m, a broad green valley with terraced fields and scattered villages. Inscriptions call the capital Semja. On a promontory above the river, a place known locally as Lamathada, stand the Kanakasundari temple and the remains of palace and settlement buildings that archaeologists have excavated in recent decades. Walking among the stone foundations, you get a sense of a royal centre that once received envoys from Tibet and the plains.

Why rule from such a remote valley? For a kingdom that controlled the trade routes between Tibet and India, the Karnali basin was not remote at all. Salt, wool and borax came down from the Tibetan plateau; grain, cloth and metal went up. Sinja sat between Jumla's fertile valley and the passes to the north, close to the trade and the grain that sustained an army.
Today Sinja is reached by a rough road from Jumla or on foot as part of the Rara Lake trek. People here say with pride that the Nepali language was born in their valley, and they are not far wrong.

sections.heading: Dullu and the first written Nepali
paras: The Khas language spoken in Sinja and across the Karnali basin is the ancestor of modern Nepali. Its earliest known written forms appear in Khasa royal inscriptions, and the most famous of these stands at Dullu in Dailekh district: a stone pillar, or kirti stambha, raised by King Prithvi Malla in the 1350s. Its text mixes Sanskrit with early Khas, Buddhist syllables with Hindu invocations, and lists the king's ancestors. Scholars treat it as one of the key documents of the Nepali language.

Dullu itself was an important centre, described in local histories as the winter capital of the Sinja kings. After the Khasa kingdom broke up, Dullu became the seat of its own small kingdom, which survived as a semi-autonomous principality inside Nepal until 1962. Around Dullu are shrines where natural gas escapes from the ground and burns as small, steady flames, and a pilgrimage circuit, the Panchkoshi, links five sacred sites around them.

To see the pillar and the flames, travellers drive from Surkhet into the Dailekh hills, about four to five hours on a winding road. A local guide is essential, both to find the sites and to explain the inscriptions.

sections.heading: Buddhist kings, Hindu gods, and Lumbini
paras: One of the most interesting things about the Khasa kings is how comfortably they moved between religions. Early rulers were strong patrons of Buddhism, linked to the monasteries of western Tibet, and Tibetan records mention them. Later kings increasingly worshipped Hindu deities. Many inscriptions begin with the Buddhist mantra om mani padme hum and continue with invocations to Hindu gods.

The clearest example is at Lumbini, the Buddha's birthplace in the Terai. In 1312 King Ripu Malla visited the site and had a line carved on the Ashoka pillar, which had then stood for more than fifteen centuries: the Buddhist mantra, followed by a wish for the long rule of Ripu Malla. The words are still visible on the pillar today, a few lines below Ashoka's original inscription. He left a similar inscription on the Ashoka pillar at Niglihawa near Kapilavastu.

Kakrebihar in Surkhet is another witness to this mixed faith. The ruined base of a stone temple stands on a forested hill above Birendranagar, surrounded by hundreds of carved blocks with Buddhist and Hindu figures. It is widely attributed to Ashoka Challa in the 13th century.

sections.heading: Reading the stones
paras: You do not need to be a historian to enjoy Khasa sites, but it helps to know what to look for. The most common monument is the dewal, a small square shrine of dressed stone with a flat or pyramidal top, often carved with panels showing a deity, a horse and rider, or the donor who paid for it. Many stand alone in fields or by trails, and some are still worshipped with flowers and red powder.

Look also for the dhunge dhara, stone water spouts set into a wall below a spring, where women still fill water pots. Several in the Jumla valley carry short inscriptions in old Nepali script, recording who built them and when. Free-standing stone pillars, like the one at Dullu, record royal deeds and genealogies. Your local guide will know which village stones are old and which are recent copies, and which can be touched and which should be left alone.

sections.heading: Breakup and the Baise kingdoms
paras: In the late 14th century the Khasa kingdom fragmented. Local rulers took control of their own valleys, and the region became a patchwork of small states known as the Baise rajya, the twenty-two kingdoms, west of the Gandaki basin, alongside the Chaubise, the twenty-four kingdoms, further east. Jumla, inheriting the prestige of Sinja, became one of the most important of the Baise states, and Doti and Dullu remained significant powers.

These small kingdoms lasted until the Gorkha conquests of the late 18th century, when Prithvi Narayan Shah's successors brought the western hills into the expanding kingdom of Nepal. Jumla fell to Gorkha forces in 1789. Ironically, the language of Gorkha, which spread across Nepal as the national tongue, was itself a descendant of the Khas speech of Sinja.
list: Sinja valley, Jumla: the capital ruins and the Kanakasundari temple at Lamathada.
Dullu, Dailekh: the pillar of Prithvi Malla and the flame shrines of the Panchkoshi.
Kakrebihar, Surkhet: the ruined stone temple on a hill above Birendranagar.
Jumla valley: carved dewal shrines and inscribed stone water spouts.
Lumbini: Ripu Malla's inscription on the Ashoka pillar.

faqs.a: The Khasa Mallas were a dynasty that ruled a kingdom centred on the Sinja valley near Jumla in western Nepal from about the 12th to the late 14th century. At their height they controlled the Karnali basin, parts of western Tibet including Purang and Guge, and hill areas east to Kaski. They are distinct from the Malla kings of the Kathmandu Valley.

faqs.q: Are the Khasa Mallas related to the Mallas of Kathmandu?
faqs.a: No. Despite the shared title Malla, which was used by several unrelated dynasties in South Asia, the Khasa Mallas of Sinja and the Malla kings of the Kathmandu Valley were separate lines. The Khasa kings even raided the valley in the late 13th and early 14th centuries, according to the Newar chronicles.

faqs.q: Where was the capital of the Khasa kingdom?
faqs.a: The capital was Sinja, also written Semja in inscriptions, in the Sinja valley of Jumla district in Karnali Province. Ruins of palaces and settlement remains stand on a promontory called Lamathada next to the Kanakasundari temple. Dullu in Dailekh is described in local histories as a winter capital.

Modern Nepali descends from the Khas language spoken in the Karnali basin, and some of its earliest written records are Khasa royal inscriptions, especially Prithvi Malla's pillar at Dullu from the 1350s. For this reason Sinja and the Karnali region are widely called the birthplace of Nepali. The language later spread east with the Gorkha kingdom.

faqs.q: What did Ripu Malla write on the Lumbini pillar?
faqs.a: In 1312 Ripu Malla had the Buddhist mantra om mani padme hum carved on the Ashoka pillar at Lumbini, followed by a wish for his long rule. The inscription is still visible below Ashoka's original text. He also left an inscription on the Ashoka pillar at Niglihawa near Kapilavastu.

faqs.q: Can I visit Khasa sites as a traveller?
faqs.a: Yes. Sinja is reached from Jumla by rough road or on the Rara Lake trek. Dullu is four to five hours by road from Surkhet. Kakrebihar is just outside Birendranagar in Surkhet. Lumbini's pillar is in the Sacred Garden. Our eight-night Khasa heritage journey links Jumla, Sinja, Surkhet and Dullu.

In Karnali and the far west, a dewal is a small square stone shrine, often carved with panels showing deities, horses or donors, many dating from the Khasa period and the Baise kingdoms that followed. You see them in fields, by trails and in villages around Jumla, Sinja and Dailekh. Some are still worshipped.

faqs.q: Why did the Khasa kingdom collapse?
faqs.a: Historians point to weaker central rulers after the 14th century, the power of regional nobles and the difficulty of holding a mountain kingdom together. The state broke into the small Baise kingdoms, including Jumla, Doti and Dullu, which lasted until the Gorkha conquests of the late 18th century.

faqs.q: When did Jumla become part of Nepal?
faqs.a: Jumla, the strongest heir of the Khasa kingdom among the Baise states, was conquered by the forces of the Gorkha kingdom in 1789 during the expansion that followed Prithvi Narayan Shah's unification. Dullu kept a degree of local autonomy as a principality until 1962.
